banner.demo: Demo mode – the data shown is made up.
why.no_user: Ingress sent no username, safe read-only mode
why.not_listed: user is in neither full_access nor read_access
dash.no_aps: No access points configured. Add them in the app configuration, see
ap.confirm_upgrade: Run {pkg} upgrade on {ap}? It may take several minutes and use overlay space.
ap.confirm_reboot: Reboot {ap}? Clients will be disconnected for 1–2 minutes.
ap.overlay_low: Only {size} left on the overlay. Upgrading several packages may not fit, better update the whole image (sysupgrade).
col.name: Name
ssid.intro: Changes are written with uci to all ticked APs. Empty field = unchanged. A preview is shown before writing.
ssid.readonly: You have read-only access, SSIDs cannot be changed.
ssid.none: No SSIDs (APs are offline or not loaded yet).
preview.title: Preview
preview.reload_note: After wifi reload, clients on the affected APs disconnect for a few seconds.
msg.no_permission: You are not allowed to do this (read-only).
msg.ui_only: Actions only from the app UI.
msg.busy: Another action is already running on this AP, wait for it to finish.
msg.reboot_sent: Reboot sent. The AP will be unreachable for about 1–2 minutes.
msg.timeout: Timed out after {s} s. The command may still be running on the AP.
msg.ssid_not_found: SSID not found, reload the page.
msg.no_change: No change (nothing selected or values are the same).
msg.preview_expired: The preview expired, create it again.
msg.reverted: Error. Uncommitted changes reverted (uci revert), check the AP.
msg.bad_ssid: The SSID must be 1–32 bytes long.
msg.bad_key: The password must be 8–63 printable ASCII characters.
denied.title: Access denied
denied.text: User {user} has no access to OpenWrt-Admin.
denied.hint: An administrator can add them in the app configuration to read_access (read-only) or full_access.
setup.key_text: The app logs in to the APs and the router with this key (reading via ubus, changes via uci). Add it to every device:
setup.key_note: /etc/dropbear/authorized_keys survives sysupgrade. After sysupgrade -n add it again (or put it in a first-boot script).
setup.devices_text: APs, user, intervals and the DHCP router are set in Home Assistant: Settings → Apps (Add-ons) → OpenWrt-Admin → Configuration.
setup.users_text: Login is handled by Home Assistant; the app decides what each HA user may do.
setup.no_roles_warning: No roles configured: every HA user who opens the panel has full access (reboot, apk, SSIDs). Set full_access and read_access in the app configuration.
setup.users_hint: Use the HA username (Settings → People → Users) or the display name; case-insensitive.
setup.lang_source.auto: automatic, from Home Assistant / the browser
setup.display_hint: Defaults for everyone are set in the app configuration (refresh_interval, language). The choices here apply to this browser only.
setup.api_text: The current state is also available as JSON:
router.not_wifi: LAN at the router or not connected
router.confirm_reboot: Reboot the router {ap}? The whole network and the internet will be down for 1–2 minutes.
router.confirm_upgrade: Run {pkg} upgrade on the router {ap}? Upgrading packages can break networking; sysupgrade is safer.
router.actions_note: Rebooting the router takes the whole network and internet down (Home Assistant keeps running but cannot reach anything outside the LAN for a moment).
map.title: Network map
map.wired_sub: active devices not on Wi-Fi or AP ports
map.note: Lines show logical connections: the AP is in the router's network and carries the listed VLANs. Wired devices and APs connected through another AP are detected from the AP switch MAC table (swconfig arl_table); where the switch cannot provide it, they stay under the router. Unmanaged switches in between are not visible. VLAN IDs come from device names (eth0.30, br-lan.10), bridge members and uci.
src.static_title: name from a static DHCP reservation on the router
setup.names_text: Names are taken in this order: the names list in the app configuration → Home Assistant (device registry by MAC, e.g. ESPHome) → DHCP on the router → static reservation on the router. IPs also for devices with a static address from the ARP tables of the router and APs.
setup.ha_off: off (ha_names: false) or the app does not run in Home Assistant
setup.names_hint: Names from Home Assistant are reloaded every 10 minutes and on app restart. Manual name: names → mac + name in the app configuration.
router.inactive_hint: Devices the router knows (DHCP lease or reservation) that are not on the network now – not on Wi-Fi, on a switch port or in an ARP table.
diag.title: Switch diagnostics (wired clients)
diag.no_arl: This AP's switch cannot list its MAC table (swconfig arl_table) – wired clients behind it stay at the router.
diag.gw_missing: The AP does not have it in its ARP table right now – the uplink cannot be detected, wired clients will not be placed until the next refresh.
diag.no_uplink: The gateway MAC is not on any switch port – the uplink cannot be detected.
diag.memory_hint: The switch forgets a MAC address after a few minutes without traffic. The app remembers the last port so the device does not jump to the router; the router also pings quiet devices now and then.
notify.title: OpenWrt-Admin: new device on the network
OpenWrt-Admin: {n} new devices on the network
upd.title: Updates
upd.release: OpenWrt {v} is available (firmware upgrades are done by hand, e.g. firmware-selector and sysupgrade).
upd.hint: Checked automatically every {h} h (apk update / opkg update), or with the Check for updates button.
upd.hint_off: Automatic check is off (update_check_hours: 0), only with the Check for updates button.
backup.title: Configuration backups
backup.hint: Automatically every {d} days, the last {k} are kept. Stored in the app's /data, so they are part of Home Assistant backups too. Contains Wi-Fi passwords and keys – only full access can download.
backup.hint_off: Automatic backups are off (backup_interval_days: 0), the last {k} are kept. The archive contains Wi-Fi passwords and keys – only full access can download.
backup.restore: Restore: upload the file to the device's /tmp and run sysupgrade -r /tmp/<file> && reboot (or LuCI Backup / Restore).
kick.title: Disconnect {who}
kick.ban_title: The block applies on all APs with the same SSID, until it expires or Wi-Fi restarts.
kick.ban_note: The block is kept in hostapd memory – a Wi-Fi or AP restart clears it. A permanent block is a MAC filter in the SSID settings.
new.title: first seen {ago}
msg.bad_request: Invalid request (the client may have disconnected meanwhile).
setup.maint_hint: Configured in the app configuration: notify_new_devices, notify_service, notify_random_mac, update_check_hours, backup_interval_days, backup_keep. On the first start all devices on the network are taken as known.
unban.title: Unblock {who}
ports.title: Ports
ports.hint: Negotiated speed and duplex from the switch (swconfig, SNMP) or network card (ubus network.device). 100 Mb/s instead of 1 Gb/s is often a faulty or 4-wire cable, or a device that cannot do more.
map.legend_speed: port speed (AP uplink, wired devices): green 1 Gb/s, orange slower
switch.snmp_hint: The switch is read over SNMP v2c (read-only). Check the IP, community and that the Home Assistant address is allowed in the switch settings (Management Station IP).
switch.gw_missing: The router MAC is not known yet (router or APs have not loaded it) – the uplink cannot be detected.
ports.only_up: Only connected ports shown ({n} disconnected hidden).
Only connected ports shown ({n} disconnected hidden).
stats.title: Network statistics
stats.no_router: Interface speeds, ping and client traffic need a router in the device list (type: router).
stats.router_error: Could not read statistics from the router: {error}
stats.ifaces_hint: RX = data the router received on the interface, TX = data it sent. On WAN, RX is the download from the internet. On LAN and VLANs, RX is what devices in the network upload and TX what they download.
stats.col_history_ping: History (green OK, orange over 100 ms, red no reply)
stats.ping_hint: Internet targets, the ISP gateway, APs and switches are pinged by the router (1 packet every {s} s). The router itself is measured by the app as the SSH response time. Internet targets are set with the ping_targets option, the rest is switched on with ping_devices.
stats.top_none: Nobody is downloading right now, or there is no data yet (the speed is the difference between two readings).
stats.source_nlbwmon: Source: nlbwmon on the router. The speed is an average over the last ~90 s, because nlbwmon refreshes its data every refresh_interval (default 30 s). "This period" = total since the start of the nlbwmon accounting period.
stats.source_conntrack: Source: conntrack on the router (connection counters), average over the last 30 s. Only IPv4 traffic between LAN/VLANs and the internet is counted. With flow offloading, part of the traffic may be missing.
stats.source_none: Client traffic is not available: traffic_source is off, or the router has neither nlbwmon nor /proc/net/nf_conntrack.
stats.wifi_hint: From the difference of transferred data reported by hostapd between two AP readings (poll_interval {s} s). Includes traffic inside the network.
stats.ports_hint: ↓ = towards the device on the port, ↑ = from the device. SNMP counters (ifHCInOctets/ifHCOutOctets). This also shows traffic between devices inside the network (e.g. laptop ↔ server) that does not pass the router. Percent = utilisation of the port speed.
stats.updated: Updated {ago}, interval {s} s, the last hour of history is kept only in the app's memory.
stats.map_load_title: Current traffic: ↓ towards the device, ↑ from the device
map.legend_load: current traffic (↓ towards the device / ↑ from it, from statistics); red and thick = over half of the port speed
col.now_title: Current speed from the difference of transferred data between two AP readings
setup.sensors_demo: demo – {n} entities prepared, nothing is sent to HA in demo mode
setup.stats_hint: Sensors are called sensor.openwrt_admin_* and binary_sensor.openwrt_admin_*. They are created on the first write through the Home Assistant REST API (without a unique_id, so they cannot be edited in the UI). They are stored in the HA history and from there in InfluxDB and Grafana.
radio.title: Radios and channels
radio.none: No AP with a radio is online.
radio.dfs_title: DFS channel: the AP has to listen for radar for a minute before transmitting and leaves the channel when radar is detected.
radio.hint: Channel, width, power and noise are the real values from iwinfo (for an "auto" channel the one the radio actually uses). Channel utilisation = how much of the time the channel is busy (own traffic, neighbouring networks, interference) from iw survey between two AP readings. Above 50 % Wi-Fi is usually noticeably slower.
radio.map_hint_24: Bar = width used by the radio (20 MHz = 5 channels). Channels 1, 6 and 11 (green) do not overlap. APs that hear each other should each use a different one.
radio.map_hint_5: Bar = width used by the radio (40/80 MHz = 2/4 channels). DFS channels (52–144) in orange. APs that hear each other should not share the same channel block.
radio.w_same: {a} and {b} use the same channel {ca} on {band} – if they hear each other, they share airtime. Give them different channels.
radio.w_overlap: {a} (channel {ca}) and {b} (channel {cb}) overlap on {band} – if they hear each other, this interferes more than the same channel. On 2.4 GHz use only 1, 6 and 11.
radio.w_auto: {ap}: {radio} has channel "auto" (now {ch}). OpenWrt picks it only at start-up and may end up on a neighbour's channel – a fixed channel is better.
radio.w_24_channel: {ap}: channel {ch} on 2.4 GHz overlaps neighbouring channels – use 1, 6 or 11.
radio.w_24_wide: {ap}: width {ht} on 2.4 GHz takes almost the whole band and disturbs others – 20 MHz recommended.
radio.w_5_narrow: {ap}: 5 GHz only {ht} (20 MHz). If the radio can do 40 MHz (HT40) or 80 MHz (VHT80), that is roughly 2× or 4× faster.
radio.w_dfs: {ap}: channel {ch} is DFS – after a Wi-Fi restart it stays silent for about a minute and moves away when radar is detected.
radio.w_busy: {ap}: the {band} channel is {p} % busy – consider another channel.
radio.w_noise: {ap}: high noise on {band} ({n} dBm) – interference nearby, consider another channel.
radio.w_power_balance: {ap}: 2.4 GHz transmits stronger ({p24} dBm) than 5 GHz ({p5} dBm) – phones then stick to the slower 2.4 GHz. Lower 2.4 GHz or raise 5 GHz.
radio.w_country_mixed: The APs have different countries ({c}) – set the same everywhere, otherwise allowed channels and power differ.
radio.w_country_missing: No country set: {aps} – set the country (correct channels and power for your regulations).
radio.scan_confirm: Scan neighbouring networks on {ap} ({band})? The radio hops between channels for a few seconds – connected clients may notice a short drop.
radio.scan_confirm_all: Scan neighbouring networks on all APs and radios? Each radio hops between channels for a few seconds – connected clients may notice a short drop.
radio.scan_off_hint: Scanning neighbouring networks is off. Turn it on with the radio_scan option (it may affect clients for a few seconds).
radio.occ_hint: Bars at the bottom = how much foreign networks occupy the channel according to the last scan (number of networks, height by signal strength; red = a network stronger than −65 dBm).
radio.w_neighbor: {ap}: on {band} channel {ch}, {n} foreign networks overlap, the strongest is {name} ({sig} dBm).
radio.w_better: {ap}: according to the scan, {band} channel {best} would be less busy (now {ch}).
radio.propose_hint: The proposal is pre-filled in the form (changed values are highlighted) – adjust it if you like, then "Preview changes" → "Apply". Channels: your APs on different channels from each other and away from channels used by neighbours according to the scan (2.4 GHz only 1/6/11). Width: 2.4 GHz 20 MHz, 5 GHz as wide as the radio can (max. 80 MHz). Power: 5 GHz the highest allowed, 2.4 GHz 3 dB lower.
radio.propose_noscan: Without a neighbour scan the proposal does not know the neighbouring networks – run "Scan surroundings" first.
radio.why_channel_clash: channel overlapped another of your APs
radio.why_power5: 5 GHz at the highest allowed power
radio.why_power24: 2.4 GHz weaker than 5 GHz (clients prefer 5 GHz)
radio.country_hint: empty = no change; set on all radios
radio.edit_hint: Only values that differ from the current settings are changed. On each AP: uci set → uci commit wireless → wifi reload; on error uci revert. Clients disconnect for a few seconds.
radio.apply_note: After wifi reload clients disconnect for a few seconds and reconnect.
radio.apply_dfs_note: DFS channel: the AP stays silent for about a minute after the change (radar check).
radio.err_channel: channel not allowed for this radio
radio.err_htmode: the radio does not support this width
radio.err_country: the country must be a two-letter code (e.g. CZ)
ssid.new_hint: A new wifi-iface section (owadmin_<ssid>_<radio>) is created on each selected radio, then uci commit wireless → wifi reload. The network must exist on the AP (for VLAN networks the AP needs the interface). WPA3 (sae) needs wpad with SAE support on the AP (wpad-basic-mbedtls and newer) and WPA3-capable clients – WPA2/WPA3 is the safe choice. The network is chosen by VLAN – each AP uses its own name for it (e.g. HOST / host); radios of an AP without that network cannot be selected.
ssid.new_note: After wifi reload clients disconnect for a few seconds. The password is never shown or logged.
ssid.err_network: {ap}: network "{net}" does not exist on the AP.
setup.user_title: Recommended: a dedicated user instead of root
setup.user_text: To see in the device log what the app did and what you did: create a user {user} with root rights (UID 0, no password – key login only) on every AP and the router. Nothing is installed:
setup.user_config: Then set ssh_user: {user} in the app configuration (or user: {user} for a single device).
setup.user_active: the app now logs in as {user}
setup.user_note: OpenWrt (dropbear) reads the keys of every UID 0 user from the same file /etc/dropbear/authorized_keys, so the key stays there. /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow survive a normal sysupgrade; after sysupgrade -n add them again (or put them in a first-boot script).
setup.audit_text: Every action (reboot, SSID, radios, apk, backup, scan, client disconnect) is also written to the device syslog with the tag openwrt-admin and the name of the Home Assistant user who started it. Passwords are never logged. On the device:
svc.intro: Services of this device and extensions (adblock, banIP) when installed. Every action shows a command preview and runs only after Apply; it is written to the device log with the user's name.
svc.readonly: Read only – you can see the service status and search why a domain or IP is blocked. Only users with full access can change things.
svc.protected_title: The app cannot connect to the device without this service – restart only (in the background).
svc.footer: Status is read when the page opens (read only, nothing is written to the device log). Services that only set something up at boot (boot, sysctl, led…) are hidden.
svc.err_action: This action is not possible for this service.
svc.note_adb_suspend: A timed pause is guarded by a timer on the router itself – blocking resumes even if Home Assistant restarts meanwhile. A router reboot cancels the pause.
svc.note_adb_list: After a list change adblock reloads (tens of seconds). Allowed domains match exactly (not subdomains). Adding to one list removes the domain from the other.
svc.note_ban_list: Adding to one list removes the address from the other. If banIP is enabled, its sets are reloaded.
svc.note_protected: The restart runs in the background after 2 s – the connection drops for a moment.
adb.warn_empty: adblock is enabled but the blocklist is empty – nothing is blocked. It was probably paused elsewhere, or the lists were not downloaded after the router booted. Use Resume blocking or Reload lists.
adb.paused_until: Paused, blocking resumes by itself in about {m} min.
adb.resume_missed: The resume time has passed but adblock is still not blocking (the timer did not run, or the router rebooted) – resume it manually.
adb.hint: The lists are /etc/adblock/adblock.allowlist and adblock.blocklist on the router (same as in LuCI). Search checks the active list and the backups of the individual lists.
ban.disabled: banIP is disabled (ban_enabled = 0) – enable it in LuCI. The lists can still be edited, they take effect once it is enabled.
ban.error: banIP is enabled but not running – nothing is blocked. Cause: logread -e banIP on the router.
ban.hint: The lists are /etc/banip/banip.allowlist and banip.blocklist on the router (IPv4/IPv6, networks in CIDR too). Search shows the set (list) containing the address.
ban.err_ip: Invalid IP address (a single address for search, a network such as 198.51.100.0/24 is fine for the lists).
dhcp.intro: Address ranges per network and static leases on the router (dnsmasq). Every change shows a preview of the uci commands, is written after Apply (uci commit dhcp, dnsmasq reload) and reverted on error. The router configuration is backed up before the first change of the day.
dhcp.readonly: Read only – only users with full access can change ranges and leases.
dhcp.warn_apknew: {file} exists on the router – the new default DHCP configuration from a package upgrade (yours was not overwritten). It usually differs only in what you configured; compare and then delete it:
dhcp.warn_tight: Only {free} of {size} addresses are left in the dynamic range of {net} – new devices may not get an address. Enlarge the range or move static leases out of it.
dhcp.no_dhcp: No DHCP – the router does not hand out addresses in this network (devices have fixed IPs).
dhcp.pools_hint: Range = network address + start to + start + count − 1 (as in LuCI). IPv6 (odhcpd) is not changed here.
dhcp.name: Name
dhcp.in_pool_title: The IP is inside the dynamic range – it works, but takes free addresses from other devices.
dhcp.static_hint: A new IP is suggested as the first free address below the dynamic range (not reserved, leased, in ARP or used by a local name). "name in DNS" = the name resolves even if the device does not send it (dns=1).
dhcp.note: After Apply: uci commit dhcp and dnsmasq reload (DNS and DHCP keep running, takes a moment). A new static IP applies once the device renews its lease (or reconnects).
dhcp.backup_failed: The backup before the change failed ({err}) – nothing was changed.
dhcp.err_name: Invalid name – letters, digits and hyphen, max. 63 characters (no spaces or underscores).
dhcp.err_ip_net: The IP is not in any router network.
dhcp.err_ip_reserved: {ip} is the network, broadcast or router address.
dhcp.err_mac_taken: MAC {mac} already has the static lease {name}.
dhcp.warn_name_dup: Another lease already has the name {name} – it will be in DNS twice.
dhcp.warn_ip_leased: {ip} is currently leased dynamically to another device ({name}, {mac}) – it may clash until that lease expires.
dhcp.warn_ip_domain: {ip} is also used by the local name {name}.
dhcp.warn_no_dhcp: The router does not serve DHCP in {net} – the lease applies once DHCP is enabled.
dhcp.warn_in_pool: {ip} is inside the dynamic range ({first}–{last}). It works but takes free addresses; free address outside the range: {free}.
dhcp.err_range: Invalid range – start ≥ 1 and start + count ≤ {max}.
dhcp.err_leasetime: Invalid lease time (e.g. 12h, 30m, 1d; at least 2 minutes).
dhcp.warn_pool_res: {n} static leases are inside the new range.
dhcp.warn_disable: Turning DHCP off in {net} stops handing out addresses (devices lose the network when their leases expire).
dhcp.apk_other: Other unmerged configurations from package upgrades: {n}
dhcp.apk_other_hint: Harmless – apk does not overwrite your modified configuration and stores the new default next to it as .apk-new. Look through the differences (copy over any new options you want by hand) and delete the files:
dns.intro: Local names and aliases resolved by the router (dnsmasq), and a lookup test. Changes go through preview and Apply (uci commit dhcp, dnsmasq reload) and are reverted on error; the router is backed up before the first change of the day.
dns.readonly: Read only – you can test lookups; only users with full access can change names.
dns.name: Name
dns.lookup_hint: Asks dnsmasq on the router just like clients do – local names, aliases, static leases and adblock all apply.
dns.names_hint: Name → address ("Hostnames" in LuCI, dhcp.@domain). It can be a bare name (then also valid as name.{dom}), a name in your own domain (server.home) or a public domain you want to point to an internal address at home (web.example.com → server in the DMZ).
dns.cnames_hint: An alias points to another name (jellyfin.lan → nas.lan). dnsmasq only answers an alias when it knows the target itself – a local name, a static or current lease; aliases to internet names do not work (? = the router does not know the target).
dns.settings_hint: Read only. The upstream servers belong to the WAN interface (network.wan.dns) – changing them restarts WAN, so this stays in LuCI (Network → Interfaces → wan, or DHCP and DNS → Forwards).
dns.err_name: Invalid name – letters, digits, hyphens and dots (e.g. nas.home).
dns.warn_multi: {name} already points to {ip} – the name will have two addresses (clients pick either).
dns.err_is_cname: {name} is already an alias (CNAME) – a name cannot be both an alias and an address.
dns.warn_ip_net: {ip} is not in any router network – make sure the address is reachable.
dns.info_bare: Name without a domain – resolves as {name} and {name}.{dom}.
dns.err_loop: An alias cannot point to itself.
dns.err_cname_is_name: {name} is already a local name with an address – the alias needs another name.
dns.warn_target: The router does not know the target {target} (not a local name or lease) – the alias will not work until the target exists.
dns.note: After Apply: uci commit dhcp and dnsmasq reload. Clients may cache the old answer for a while – the lookup test shows the router's answer right away.
dns.wan_unused: WAN servers are not used – noresolv
dns.a_hint: They take precedence over the WAN servers (noresolv=1) and change with a dnsmasq reload only – no internet outage. Empty field = back to the WAN servers. After saving the router tries to resolve nic.cz; if that fails it restores the previous settings.
dns.fwd_hint: Queries for the domain (and its subdomains) go to the given server – e.g. a company domain behind a VPN. This is server=/domain/ip in dnsmasq, changed with a dnsmasq reload only.
dns.b_warn: The change is written to network.wan.dns and means a network reload – the internet may drop for a few seconds (LAN and Wi-Fi keep running). After the reload the router tries to resolve nic.cz; if that fails it restores the previous servers. If servers are set in dnsmasq, they take precedence and these are not used.
dns.err_no_wan: The router has no wan interface.
dns.err_none_answer: None of the servers answered the router – the change would leave the network without DNS.
dns.warn_noanswer: No answer from: {s}. Check the address; dnsmasq will use the other servers.
dns.warn_port: A server with its own port (local DoH/DoT proxy) is not tested in advance.
dns.warn_wan_unused: Own servers are set in dnsmasq (noresolv) – the WAN servers will not be used until you remove them from dnsmasq.
dns.shown_check: # then: nslookup nic.cz 127.0.0.1 – if it fails, the previous settings are restored
dns.applied_ok: OK – nic.cz resolves through the router.
dns.rolled_back: nic.cz did not resolve after the change – previous settings restored.
dns.do_up_wan: remove upstream DNS from dnsmasq – back to the WAN servers
dns.note_up: After Apply: uci commit dhcp, dnsmasq reload and a nic.cz lookup check (with automatic rollback).
dns.note_wan: After Apply: uci commit network and a network reload – the internet may drop for a few seconds. Then a nic.cz lookup check, rolled back to the previous servers on failure.
fw.loading: Loading the firewall from the router…
fw.intro: Zones, forwardings, rules and port forwards on the router (fw4) and what of it is reachable from the internet. Blocking devices, port forwards, turning rules on and off and the zone map by clicking – every change with a safety net: if the app cannot reconnect after the change, the router reverts within 90 s.
fw.w_wan_input: The WAN interface is in the zone "{zone}" with input ACCEPT – everything not blocked by a rule on the router is reachable from the internet. Open services: {ports}.
fw.w_wan_forward: The zone "{zone}" (WAN) has forward ACCEPT – the router also passes traffic from the internet into internal networks if it arrives.
fw.w_net_multi: Network {net} is in several zones ({zones}) – only the first, "{first}", applies; rules of the other zones do not.
fw.w_dev_multi: Interface {dev} is in several zones ({zones}) – input and forward go to the first, "{first}".
fw.w_no_masq: The WAN zone has no masquerading (masq) – internal networks cannot reach the internet unless NAT is done elsewhere.
fw.w_include: {path} – an old fw3 include that fw4 ignores (no fw4_compatible). You can delete it.
fw.svc_open: nothing blocks it – zone {zone} input is ACCEPT
fw.nothing_open: Nothing is open from the internet.
fw.services_hint: From netstat on the router: services on all addresses or on the public IP and how the firewall sees them from the internet.
fw.matrix: Zone map – who may go where
fw.matrix_hint: Column "router" = input to the router itself (zone input policy). Other columns = forwarding between zones; the diagonal shows the forward policy inside the zone. "+ rules" = exceptions for specific ports or addresses.
fw.name: Name
fw.filter_ph: name, zone, port, IP or MAC
fw.rules_hint: Order follows the configuration – the first matching rule wins. Adding and editing rules and blocking devices come in later versions.
fw.custom_hint: Files in /etc/nftables.d/ are loaded into the fw4 table; the app only shows them and does not change them.
fw.warn_open: Turning on "{name}" opens port {port} from the internet.
fw.note: Saved with a safety net: the router backs up its firewall configuration, checks it (fw4 check) and reloads. The app then reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the router reverts after 90 s.
fwd.hint: The port from the internet can be a single port or a range (5000-5010); the inside port must have a range of the same size, empty = the same. The destination zone is found from the IP. "Only from" limits access to one IP or network (CIDR) – recommended for sensitive services. New port forwards are stored in a named section owa_fwd_…; those created in LuCI can be edited and deleted too.
fwd.note: Saved with a safety net: the router backs up its firewall configuration, checks it (fw4 check) and reloads. The app then reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the router reverts after 90 s. Connections that are already open keep the old behaviour until they expire.
fwd.do_add: new port forward "{name}": port {port} from the internet → {to} (zone {zone})
fwd.do_edit: edit port forward "{name}": port {port} from the internet → {to} (zone {zone})
fwd.err_name: Enter a name (letters, digits, space, . : + - ( ) /, at most 40 characters).
fwd.err_port: Invalid port "{v}" – a number 1–65535 or a range from-to.
fwd.err_range: The inside port range must be the same size as the port range from the internet.
fwd.err_src: "{v}" is not an IPv4 address or network (e.g. 198.51.100.7 or 198.51.100.0/24).
fwd.err_ip_net: IP {ip} is not in any of the router's networks – ports can only be forwarded to devices on the local network.
fwd.err_ip_wan: IP {ip} is on the WAN network (zone {zone}) – ports can only be forwarded into the local network.
fwd.err_dup: The port is already forwarded by "{name}" ({port}). Two forwards on the same port do not work – edit or turn off the existing one.
fwd.w_router_svc: The router listens on port {port} ({prog}). From the internet the port will then lead to the target device, not to the router.
fwd.w_risky: Port {ports} is often attacked from the internet. Consider access over a VPN, or at least "Only from".
fwd.w_dynamic: {ip} is not a static DHCP lease. If the device has its IP set manually that is fine; otherwise it may get a different address later and the forward stops working – give it a static lease.
fwd.w_still_off: The port forward is turned off and stays off after the edit.
fwd.lock_accept: Rule "{name}" allows port {port} from zone {zone}, which this app uses to connect to the router (SSH). Without it the app will most likely not connect – it will not confirm the change and the router reverts after 90 s.
fwd.lock_block: Rule "{name}" blocks port {port} from zone {zone}, which this app uses to connect to the router (SSH). Once on, the app will most likely not connect – it will not confirm the change and the router reverts after 90 s.
fwd.lock_redirect: The forward sends port {port} from zone {zone} elsewhere – that is the port this app uses to connect to the router (SSH). The app would lose the connection; the router reverts after 90 s.
fwd.lock_ha_block: {mac} is the device this app connects from (Home Assistant). It loses internet access (updates, cloud integrations); managing the router keeps working.
zm.hint: Click a cell to switch it (changed cells are dashed); "Preview changes" then saves them all at once with the safety net.
zm.note: Saved with a safety net: the router backs up its firewall configuration, checks it (fw4 check) and reloads. The app then reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the router reverts after 90 s. Rules ("+ N rules") take precedence and still apply. A forwarding is one-way – replies to allowed connections always pass.
zm.do_in_on: allow input from zone {zone} to the router (input ACCEPT)
zm.do_in_off: deny input from zone {zone} to the router (input REJECT)
zm.c_wan_input: Zone {zone} receives traffic from the internet – the router becomes reachable from the whole internet on every port it listens on (SSH, LuCI, DNS…).
zm.c_wan_fwd: Zone {src} receives traffic from the internet – the whole internet gets access to zone {dest} and all its devices.
zm.c_wan_zfwd: Zone {zone} receives traffic from the internet – it will pass the router back into this zone's networks.
zm.c_lock: This app connects to the router from zone {zone} (SSH, port {port}) and no rule allows that port. The app will most likely not connect – it will not confirm the change and the router reverts after 90 s.
zm.w_fwd: All devices in zone {src} will see all devices in zone {dest}. For access to only some of them a rule is better.
zm.w_rules: Rule exceptions ({n}) still apply to {src} → {dest} – they take precedence.
zm.w_in_rules: Rule exceptions ({n}) still apply to input from zone {zone} – they take precedence.
zm.w_dhcp_dns: No rule allows {what} from zone {zone} – its devices will not get an address or resolve names. Add rules (like "Allow-DHCP") or keep input allowed.
zm.w_mixed: Zone {zone} contains WAN and other networks ({nets}) – the change applies to all of them. Better put WAN in its own zone.
zm.w_empty: Zone {zone} has no interface – the change has no effect for now.
safe.failed: The change was not made (error in the commands or the check) – the configuration is unchanged.
safe.armed: Change saved with a safety net ({s} s), waiting for a new connection…
safe.not_confirmed: Could not reconnect to the device after the change – it reverts to the previous configuration within {s} s of saving.
safe.shown: # safety net: backup, 90 s countdown, confirm over a new connection, otherwise rollback
fw.w_fw3: The router uses the older fw3 firewall (OpenWrt 21.02 and older) – the overview is limited: no real zone order per interface and no fw4 checks. Rules and port forwards are shown, the app will not change them.
blk.title: Blocked devices
blk.expired: should have ended – the router was probably off, remove manually
blk.label: Label
blk.hint: Blocks internet access by MAC (a firewall rule with REJECT to the WAN zone; the device keeps working on the home network). Time is handled by cron on the router in its local time: a schedule turns the rule on and off (across midnight the next morning), a temporary block deletes itself at the given minute. Works even while Home Assistant is off. Phones with a random (private) MAC must be blocked by the MAC they use on that Wi-Fi.
blk.link_title: Block internet for this device (router firewall)
blk.err_nomac: Pick a device or enter a MAC.
blk.err_nowan: Could not determine the WAN zone – cannot block.
blk.err_duration: The duration must be 5 minutes to 14 days.
blk.err_until: The end must be in the future (router time now {now}) and at most 60 days ahead.
blk.err_schedule: A schedule needs from and to times (HH:MM, different) and at least one day.
blk.now_on: Now is inside the schedule – the block starts immediately.
blk.now_off: Now is outside the schedule – the block starts at the from time.
blk.warn_already: The device is already blocked by the rule “{name}”.
blk.warn_random: {mac} looks like a random (private) MAC – the phone may change it after a Wi-Fi change or over time and the block stops working.
blk.do_del: unblock: {name} (delete the rule and its schedule)
blk.note: Saved with the safety net (firewall and crontab). Schedules and temporary blocks are then run by cron on the router – independently of the app.
blk.fwtime_title: The rule has time conditions in fw4 itself – whether it applies now depends on the time; fw4 may not use local time or ranges across midnight.
blk.only_ports: only ports {ports} {proto} – not the whole internet
vl.title: VLANs and networks
vl.loading: Reading networks from the router and APs…
vl.all_ok: Nothing suspicious – VLANs, bridges and SSIDs match.
vl.n_not_uplink: only on the device's ports, not on the uplink
vl.hint: Rows follow how traffic goes over the cable to the router (uplink): a VLAN number or "untagged". Network names may differ between devices; they are matched by VLAN. For each device: the network (address, or "none" = bridging only), 📶 SSIDs with bands (struck through = disabled), 🔌 ports where the VLAN is available, and the bridge. Read-only – nothing changes; keys and passwords are filtered out on the device.
vl.switch: Switch between the router and the APs
vl.switch_text: The app reads a managed switch between the router and the APs over SNMP when it is configured (option switches) – it then gets its own column and the ports to the router and APs are checked. Without it: for a VLAN to get from the router to an AP, the switch must carry every VLAN from the table tagged (T) on the port to the router and on the ports to the APs that use it; "untagged" = the VLAN the port has as PVID (untagged, usually 1). A port to an end device in one network (e.g. a server in the DMZ) has that VLAN untagged and as PVID. Writing to the switch over SNMP is a possible future extension.
vl.e_two_bridges: {dev} is in two bridges ({brs}). Only one applies (by start order) – the networks may get joined together, or one bridge stays disconnected. Keep it in one only.
vl.e_no_switch_vlan: {dev} is used, but VLAN {vid} is not configured on the device's switch (swconfig / bridge-vlan) – traffic will not pass.
vl.e_ssid_no_iface: SSID {ssid} is assigned to network {net}, which does not exist.
vl.e_ssid_split: SSID {ssid} leads to different networks ({nets}) – a client gets a different network depending on the band.
vl.e_not_on_router: {vid} is used by {devs}, but the router does not have it – its traffic leads nowhere.
vl.e_ssid_vlans: SSID {ssid} leads to different VLANs on different APs ({where}) – when roaming between APs a client ends up in a different network.
vl.w_raw_cpu: Bridge {br} contains {eth} as well as its VLANs ({eth}.N). The switch CPU port is tagged, bare {eth} is useless – {eth}.1 is enough.
vl.w_multi_gw: A default gateway is set on several networks ({ifaces}) – the device has several default routes. An AP needs a gateway only in the management network.
vl.w_ssid_local: SSID {ssid} leads to network {net}, which is on no VLAN or port – clients stay within the AP.
vl.w_ap_ip: Network {iface} (VLAN {vid}) has address {ip} on the AP – the AP is reachable from that network too (SSH, LuCI). If the AP only bridges it, set proto "none" (unmanaged).
vl.w_no_cpu: VLAN {vid} on the switch has no CPU port – the AP only passes it between ports and does not see it itself.
vl.w_subnet: {dev}: {iface} has address {ip}, but the router has network {net} in this VLAN ({vid}).
nw.title: New network on the router ({router})
nw.name: Network name
nw.delete: Delete the network with its DHCP, zone and VLAN
nw.no_trunk: The router has no port with VLANs and no bridge with VLAN filtering (bridge-vlan). Turn on VLAN filtering in LuCI first (Network → Interfaces → Devices → bridge → Bridge VLAN filtering) – the app does not turn it on itself because that changes the whole LAN.
nw.hint: The VLAN method follows the router: with DSA a new bridge-vlan section (interface <bridge>.<VLAN>), with swconfig a new VLAN on the switch and a bridge br-<network>, on a port without a switch a device <port>.<VLAN> and a bridge br-<network>. A new zone is isolated: internet yes (optional), other networks no, to the router only DHCP and DNS. Everything is saved at once with the safety net. New sections are named owa_…_<network>.
nw.note: Saved with a safety net: the router backs up network, dhcp and firewall, checks the firewall (fw4 check), reloads network, DHCP and firewall. The app then reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the router reverts after 90 s.
nw.do_dhcp: DHCP: addresses from .{start}, {limit} addresses, 12 h lease
nw.do_zone_new: new zone "{zone}": internet ({wan}) yes, other networks no, to the router only DHCP and DNS
nw.do_zone_new_noinet: new zone "{zone}" without internet, to the router only DHCP and DNS
nw.err_unreadable: Could not read the router's settings (networks or firewall) – try "Reload".
nw.err_name: "{v}" – the name must start with a letter, only letters, digits and _, at most 12 characters (not lan, wan, loopback).
nw.err_name_used: Network "{v}" already exists on the router.
nw.err_dhcp_used: DHCP section "{v}" already exists – choose another name.
nw.err_ports: Choose at least one port where the VLAN will be tagged (usually the uplink to the switch).
nw.err_cidr: "{v}" – enter the router address with a mask, e.g. 192.168.50.1/24 (mask /16 to /30).
nw.err_overlap: Network {v} overlaps {u}, which the router already has.
nw.err_pool: The DHCP range does not fit into the network (at most {max} addresses).
nw.err_zone: "{v}" – the zone name must start with a letter, only letters, digits and _, at most 11 characters.
nw.err_zone_used: Zone "{v}" already exists – choose another name, or "into zone".
nw.err_fw4: Networks can only be created on a router with the fw4 firewall (OpenWrt 22.03 and newer).
nw.err_del_reserved: The app does not delete network "{v}" (lan / wan / loopback).
nw.err_del_mgmt: This app connects to the router over network "{v}" – it cannot be deleted from here.
nw.err_del_proto: The app does not delete network "{v}" ({p}) – only networks with or without an address (static / none / dhcp).
nw.w_public: {v} is not a private range – local networks use 10.x, 172.16–31.x or 192.168.x.
nw.w_pool_router: The router address {ip} is inside the DHCP range – dnsmasq will not hand it out, but a range outside it is clearer.
nw.w_no_inet: The network will have no internet access.
nw.w_zone_trusted: Zone "{zone}" allows input to the router – devices in the new network get the same router access as the rest of that zone.
nw.w_no_zone: The network will be in no zone – fw4 drops its traffic (by the default policy) until you add it to a zone.
nw.w_next: The router will send VLAN {vid} only tagged on the chosen ports. To reach the APs, the switch (tagged on the ports to the router and APs) and the APs need it too – that is the next step.
nw.w_ap_has: APs already have VLAN {vid}: {aps} – they will connect once it is created.
nw.c_del_aps: These APs use this VLAN: {aps}. Their SSIDs and ports in it stop working (left without the router).
nw.w_del_hosts: The network has {n} static leases ({names}) – they stay in DHCP but will not apply.
nw.w_del_clients: Devices in network "{name}" lose their connection.
vl.w_sw_unmapped: Could not find which switch port {dev} is on (its MAC is not in the switch table, no port description matches) – its port is not checked. A port description with the device name helps.
vl.e_sw_native: Port {port} to {dev} has VLAN {u} untagged, but the router's native network is VLAN {vid} – {dev} will be in the wrong network.
vl.e_sw_untagged: Port {port} to {dev} has VLAN {vid} untagged, but {dev} expects it tagged – set T on the switch.
vl.e_sw_missing: Port {port} to {dev} does not carry VLAN {vid}, which {dev} uses – add it on the switch as tagged (T).
vl.w_sw_extra: Port {port} to {dev} also carries VLAN {vids}, which {dev} does not use – harmless, but can be removed.
vl.e_sw_router_port: VLAN {vid} is on switch ports but not on the port to the router ({port}) – its traffic cannot reach the router.
vl.w_sw_multi_u: Port {port} has several VLANs untagged ({vids}) – a device on it cannot tell which network it belongs to.
vl.w_sw_pvid: Port {port} has PVID {pvid} but VLAN {u} untagged – incoming traffic goes to VLAN {pvid}, outgoing comes from VLAN {u}.
ap.delete: Remove the VLAN from the AP
ap.note: Each AP is saved separately with the safety net: it backs up network, reloads the network and the app reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the AP reverts after 90 s. If one AP fails, the next ones are not changed.
ap.do_add: {ap}: VLAN {vid} as network "{name}" without an address (bridge only) over {how}
ap.err_router: The router does not have VLAN {vid} – create it on the router first (New network).
ap.err_method: Could not tell how VLANs go on {ap} (no switch, no DSA with bridge-vlan, no single port) – set it up in LuCI.
ap.err_uplink: Could not find the uplink on {ap} (the port with VLANs to the router) – set it up in LuCI.
ap.err_del_ssid: An SSID is connected to network "{v}" ({ssids}) – move it to another network or delete it first.
ap.err_del_native: Network "{v}" is native (untagged) – the app does not remove it from an AP.
ap.w_switch: Port {port} on switch {sw} to {ap} does not carry VLAN {vid} yet – add it there as tagged (T), otherwise traffic will not reach the AP.
ap.w_switch_generic: If {ap} is connected through a managed switch, its port must carry VLAN {vid} tagged (T).
ap.w_reload: The AP's network reloads – clients on the AP disconnect for a few seconds (on an AP with a switch also wired devices on its ports).
ap.w_next: The network on the AP has no SSID yet – connecting an SSID is the next step (SSID page).
ssid.err_vlan_missing: {ap} does not have network {net} – add it to the AP first (VLAN page).
ssid.w_move: Clients on the moved SSID reconnect into the new network – they get an address from it and its zone rules apply.
rl.hint: Rules apply in order – the first one that matches wins. Put an exception (e.g. "allow one IP to the internet") above the general rule ("block the whole network from the internet"). IPs and networks can be separated by spaces, with ! for "except". Rules with options the form does not know (time, ICMP types, limits…) can only be turned on/off, moved and deleted; edit them in LuCI.
rl.note: Saved with a safety net: the router backs up its firewall configuration, checks it (fw4 check) and reloads. The app then reconnects and confirms; if it cannot, the router reverts after 90 s. Connections that are already open are not cut by the rule until they expire.
rl.at_end: position: at the end (after all other rules)
rl.err_ip: "{v}" – enter an IP or network (192.168.10.5, 10.10.20.0/24), several separated by spaces, ! = except.
rl.err_mac: "{v}" – MAC as aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, several separated by spaces.
rl.err_port: "{v}" – port 1–65535 or a range from-to, several separated by spaces.
rl.err_port_proto: A port can only be set with TCP or UDP.
rl.err_family: Do not mix IPv4 and IPv6 in one rule.
rl.err_extra: The rule has options the app's form does not know ({opts}) – edit it in LuCI; here it can be turned on/off, moved and deleted.
rl.c_wan_router: Allows access from the internet (zone {zone}) to the router itself: {what}. Often attacked services in range: {risky}.
rl.c_wan_zone: Allows access from the internet (zone {zone}) into zone {dest} without limiting the destination IP – for one service a port forward is better.
rl.w_wan_ip: Allows access from the internet (zone {zone}) to {ip}.
rl.w_noop_allow: Zone {src} is already allowed to {dest} – the rule changes nothing by itself (it only makes sense as an exception above a blocking rule).
rl.w_noop_block: Zone {src} is already denied to {dest} – the rule changes nothing by itself (it only makes sense above an allowing rule).
rl.w_shadow: The earlier rule "{name}" with the opposite action matches everything this one does – this rule never applies. Move it up.
rl.w_shadows: This rule will be above "{name}" with the opposite action and shadow it – "{name}" never applies then. Put this rule lower, or "{name}" higher.
rl.w_default: "{name}" is a default OpenWrt rule – without it DHCP, ping or IPv6 may not work.
rl.w_move_matters: "{name}" and "{other}" have opposite actions – the order matters if they match the same traffic.
